text: JavaScript's official name is ECMAScript, and ES6, also called ES2015, was a major update that added most of the syntax this course now treats as completely normal — let and const, arrow functions, template literals, classes, and more. Every modern blockchain library — ethers.js, viem, Hardhat — is written in and expects this syntax, so this lesson makes it explicit before moving faster through the rest of Chapter Two.

Lesson three said to avoid var — here's precisely why. var is scoped to the nearest function, so it leaks out of if blocks and loops in ways that cause real, hard-to-track bugs, printing a value that should have stayed trapped inside that block. let and const are scoped to the nearest block, the curly braces they're actually declared inside, which matches what every other modern language does and what you'd genuinely expect.

A class bundles data with behavior that operates on it. constructor runs exactly once, at the moment a new instance is created with the new keyword, and this refers to that specific instance's own data — so each Wallet you create keeps its own address and balance completely separate from every other Wallet instance.

The ternary operator is condition, question mark, value if true, colon, value if false — a compact one-line form of a simple if/else that assigns a value either way without the extra lines a full if/else block would need. It reads a little awkward at first but becomes natural quickly, and you'll see it constantly once you start reading real codebases.

ES6 is the baseline every blockchain library assumes you already know: proper block scoping instead of var's leaky scoping, classes for bundling data with behavior, and the ternary operator for compact conditionals. Next up: arrow functions and destructuring — two more ES6 features you'll use in nearly every line of real code from here on.
